label: paragraph_title
text: TRAGIC DEATH.

label: text
text: MYSTERIOUS DIVING ACCIDENT.

label: text
text: LIFE LINE SNAPS.

label: text
text: EUROPEAN'S FLUCKY DIVE INTO DANGER ZONE.

label: text
text: A Chinese diver met his death under tragic but mysterious circumstances while engaged at work behind the Hongkong Electric Company's installation at North Point on Saturday forenoon.

label: text
text: The water for cooling the condensers is drawn from the sea and is treated by four circulating suction pumps near the sea wall. Two of the pumps had been put out of action for the purpose of cleaning the grating through which the water flows into the circulating system and work had been proceeding for some days.

label: text
text: The diver dressed in full gear went down the ladder as usual on Saturday morning to carry out the work in a depth of water estimated at about 12 feet. It is said that the man who was holding the life line felt a sudden pull on the rope and a length of about six feet was wrenched away from his hand at the time the diver was expected to have touched bottom. Surmising that something had happened, the man attempted to haul up the life line, but met with resistance. Having given the alarm he continued to pull until the rope broke by coming in contact with the coping of the sea wall.

label: text
text: The alarm brought to the scene Mr. W. R. Smith, of the generating station staff, who was in the office at the time. Divesting himself of his superfluous clothing, Mr. Smith dived in with a rope, which he fastened to the diver, and with many hands atthe rope the man was drawn to the surface in a helpless condition.

label: text
text: As the work of removing the man's rubber suit would have taken some time and every minute was valuable in saving his life, the suit was torn open and the head piece was quickly removed. It is stated that the man was unconscious, but shewed signs of breathing, and the only injury to his body was a bruise on his forehead. Medical assistance was summoned and in the meantime artificial respiration was applied, but the efforts of the rescuers proved to be of no avail, as the doctors who arrived soon after pronounced the man to be dead. Sir E. Stuart Taylor, M.D. was present, but declined at that stage to give an opinion as to the cause of the man's death.

label: text
text: The water is fed through 26 inch diameter pipes at the foot of the circulating pumps, and it is surmised that the diver for some unknown reason turned in the direction of the nearest of the two pumps which were working and was drawn by suction to the pipe head.

label: text
text: The force of the impact with some object under the water must have been considerable, as the copper head piece which was seen by a "Mail" man was badly dented on the head and the vision glasses were partly torn from the frame, allowing water to flow through. The condition of this part of the diving gear points to the man having been drawn head first and he was apparently rendered unconscious almost immediately after the impact.

label: text
text: It is clear that Mr. Smith undertook a very risky venture in diving down and reaching the man in a spot which as has already been seen was attended with danger. It is stated that had he waited for the remaining pumps to be stopped before going down, much time would have been lost and the electric supply would have been cut off.

label: text
text: In the course of inquiries it was stated that the deceased belonged to a family of experienced divers, his brother being in the employment of the Netherlands Harbour Works, and that he had been in the service of the Hongkong Electric Company for many years. The Electric Company, however, states definitely that the man has not been working for them.

label: paragraph_title
text: “NEAR” SWATOW.

label: text
text: REPORTED ANTI-RED MOVES.

label: text
text: CHAN COMING BACK?

label: text
text: Reports are current in the Colony that there is considerable activity in such districts as Wai Loi, which form the hinterland of Swatow, generally known as the East River region.

label: text
text: Scattered here and there are different armies — varying in strength—under General Chan Kwing-ming's banner. United, they would be a formidable force. At present they are, according to a staff officer seen this morning by a "China Mnil" reporter, reorganising and resting.

label: text
text: It was even stated that the Bolshevik hold on Swatow had been checked but this may be premature. However, there seems little doubt that troops have been on the move, and to the advantage of the anti-Red forces.

label: text
text: The staff officer interviewed also told the "China Mail" that General Chan Kwing-ming was expected to sail from Shanghai very shortly, for Hongkong, to go up-country.

label: text
text: Certain significance is also attached to a number of very high military officers having passed through recently.

label: paragraph_title
text: MATE'S WAGES.

label: paragraph_title
text: outline

label: text
text: ORDER 1N RESPECT OF S.S. "ANJOUT"

label: text
text: On the grounds that it had been impossible for the ship to do any business, the manager of the company owning the s.s. "Anjon," applied for a stay of execution in respect of an order made against him in the Supreme Court this morning. This was for the payment to the Chief Officer of the ship of wages amounting to $492.

label: text
text: Mr. T. Addis, instructed by Mr. W. B. Hind, was for the "plaintiff and the claim was not contested.

label: text
text: Chief Officer John Suiter Wilson formally proved the claim, stating that he joined the ship on July 11, and left on August 24, during which time he had been paid nothing. His study was $290 a month.

label: text
text: The Chief Justice refused the application for a stay of execution.

label: paragraph_title
text: BURIAL AT SEA.

label: text
text:
AST TRIBUTE TO CAPTAIN
JAMES SCOTT.

label: text
text: The “Straits Times” records the death of Captain James Smith Scott, a very well-known figure in shipping circles at Singapore who passed away at the Grosvenor Hotel.

label: text
text: The late Captain Scott, who was aged 69, was probably the doyen of Straits skippers. He first came in Singapore in 1871, and he had been connected with the port ever since, having commanded many vessels during that time. His last ship was the "Ban Teck Guan," running between Singapore and Malacca, and he retired from the sea six months ago.

label: text
text: It had always been Captain Scott's express desire that he should be buried at sea, and his wish was respected, the burial taking place in the main strait off Singapore.

label: text
text: The Government launch "Mars" left Johnston's Pier at eight o'clock with a large gathering of friends of the deceased on board, while many others were left behind on the pier. The launch proceeded a distance of about five miles in the direction of Pulau Samboe, where the burial service was read by the Rev. G. H. Douglas and the weighted coffin consigned to the deep.

label: text
text: Among those on board were Mr. Upton, of the P.W.D. in Johore, the deceased's son-in-law, Captain Leighton, representing the Straits Merchant Service Guild, Captain Snow, representing the Pilots Association, and Capt. Chambers senior boarding officer at Singa

label: paragraph_title
text: SHARE DEAL:

label: text
text: CLIENT AND BROKER ATLAW.

label: text
text: MISENT PLAINTIFF

label: text
text:
A deal in shares which the plaintiff claimed had not matured because of the alleged misappropriation of defendant was to have been heard in the Supreme Court this morning but plaintiff did not put in an appearance. Mr. W. B., Hind, who was instructed to him, said that he had heard he, but gone to Cantons.
The deal in question was between Cheung Cheuk-flap (plaintiff) and Pún Mang-hun in respect of 600 Green Island Cement shares. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant was acting as his agent when he bought the shares and that he refused to re-deliver them when the plaintiff paid principal and interest. The terms of the agreement, claimed plaintiff, were that $2,000 was paid by him to the defendant and the balance $13,000 was advanced by the defendant, on account, at its rate of interest of $11 per mil. " per month against the security of the shares.

label: text
text: As against the $15,000 paid for the $600 Green Island Cement shares, the plaintiff alleged that he sold them for $18,600 only to find that the defendant would not redeliver them on payment of interest and principal. "Plaintiff" therefore claimed - $8,600, this representing the value of the shares on the day in question, less $10,000 amount due to the defendant.

label: text
text: The case was adjourned until Saturday morning for the plaintiff to show cause why the case should not be struck out of the list.

label: text
text: The Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., (instructed by Hastings, Hastings, Dennis and Bowley) appeared for the defendant.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE WEATHER.

label: paragraph_title
text:
BALINTANG CHANNEL
TYPHOON.

label: paragraph_title
text: "FINE" FORECAST.

label: text
text: First reported almost stationary and now stated to be inclining slowly Northward, a typhoon is near the Balintang Channel, which is the southern of the two passages which separate the Philippines from Formosa. It is through these channels, the Balintang and the Bashi, that most of the big typhoons that strike Hongkong, enter the South China Sea from the outer Pacific.

label: text
text: The position indicated is a good distance from the 300 miles radius. As the depression is going towards the North, the danger is not apparent.

label: text
text: At any rate, the forecast for the 24 hours ending at noon tomorrow reads: — North winds, moderate; fine.

label: text
text: For the Formosa Channel, the forecast is: — North winds, strong.

label: text
text: It is interesting to note that near Amoy yesterday the wind force registered about 7 (Beaufort scale) which is fairly strong blowing.

label: paragraph_title
text: TRAFFIC ACCIDENTS.

label: paragraph_title
text: TRAMS AND LORRIES COLLIDE.

label: text
text:
In the report of week-end accidents appear two collisions between motor lorries and tram carsyone at Shaukiwan Road and the other at Wong Nel Chong Road near the race course. In each case the hand rails of the tram cars were damaged.
A fracture of the right leg was sustained by an old Chinese woman when she was knocked down by a taxi at Poldulam Road.
At Bulkeley Street, Hunghom, a Chinese woman emerged from the rear of a stationary motor bus and walked into a moving vehicle. She was knocked down and sustained slight injuries.

label: text
text: For throwing coal into the barbour with ulterior motives, a Chinese was sentenced to a month's hard labour at the Maine Court this morning.

label: paragraph_title
text: HONAM” BLINDED

label: paragraph_title
text: CURIOUS SIDELIGHT ON CHINESE MENTALITY.

label: text
text: VOYAGE 1 N°IDENTS.

label: text
text: Jinks and boats with eyes painted on the bows are by no means uncommon in Chinese waters. That the superstition which caused them to be placed there when the vessels were built so that they could see their way to port is still firmly implanted in the minds of some Chinese, is demonstrated by the trouble which has been taken to perform an optical operation on the s.s. "Honam."

label: text
text: Since the "Honam" was built some forty-five, years ago, two eyes, placed there in conformity with the old custom, have embellished the port and starboard sides, but during Saturday night the one on the port paddling box was removed. That this was done deliberately presumably in the hope that minus one eye the "Honam" would not be able to continue her runs to Canton is obvious from the thoroughness of the "operation," a panel nine feet by six and of considerable thickness, having been removed.

label: text
text: The "Honam" at the time was living at the local wharf of the Steambout Company after her latest voyage to Canton. The strike picketing experienced at Canton was more strict than ever, and not a Chinese passenger of the forty taken up was able to land. A special motor boat accompanied by an armed escort took off a number of missionaries returning to the Canton Christian College, and launches sent for other. European passengers wishing to land on Shumeen were not interfered with. The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyonk was one of the European passengers. His trip was undertaken in connection with the business of the steamboat company, but he could not say anything regarding the policy of the Company in connection with the future running of the "Honam" until he had discussed the matter at a meeting of the Board of Directors. For the present the "Honam" will continue her Hongkong-Canton service as usual.

label: text
text: Whilst in Shameen, Mr. Holyook and Mr. McI. Messer discussed the present situation with Sir James Jamieson, the British Consul-General.

label: paragraph_title
text: Today's Trip.

label: text
text: This morning very few Chinese passengers and no cargo went up. A number of missionaries who had arrived by the “President Adams” went up as did some Indian merchants and Japanese. The few Chinese who did go travelled second class and bore the appearance of servants.

label: paragraph_title
text: STOWAWAYS.

label: paragraph_title
text: FREE TRIP TO SAN FRANCISCO.

label: text
text: FILÍPINOS IN COURT.

label: text
text: Three Filipinos were brought before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning on a charge of stowing away from Manila on board the S.S. "President Cleveland."

label: text
text: One of the accused pleaded guilty and said that he intended going to San Francisco.

label: text
text: His Worship said that he would like to hear the evidence of the chief officer of the vessel, but Inspector Cashman stated that this was not possible as the boat arrived from Manila on Friday and sailed the following day. The Inspector added that the prisoners were not handed over to the Police until 3 p.m. on Saturday.

label: text
text: The accused were acquitted of the offence, the Magistrate remarking that the ship's officers had acted in a high handed manner, and they will be sent back to Manila.

label: paragraph_title
text: ARMY DECIMATED.

label: text
text: EX-CANTON "STRONG MAN" ROUTED

label: text
text: CAMPAIGN IN KWANGSI.

label: text
text: General Fan Shek-sang's army of Yunnanese mercenaries has been decimated in Kwangsi province, according to a report in the "Kung Sheung Yat Po."

label: text
text: This general was once the strong man of Canton but he took his army away to wreak revenge on Tuchun Tang Chi-yao of Yunnan.

label: text
text: Several actions were fought in "neutral" ground, i.e., Kwangsi and at one time Tuchun Tang was in danger of defeat, Tang was also reported as desirous of entering Kwangtung and driving the Kuomintang from Canton but General Fan stood in his way.

label: text
text: Subsequently fortunes fluctuated. Fan got close to the Yunnan border but fell back. The vernacular paper now says that his following has been totally routed at different places and is no longer a fighting force.

label: text
text: It was popularly said of Fan that he abandoned Canton at the height of his power because he had a superstition that no Yunnan warlord could enrich himself in Canton and stay for more than two years.

label: text
text: Activity by General Lau Tsunwan, the defeated chief of the Kwangsi army in Canton, is also reported by the same paper.

label: paragraph_title
text: UNCHANGED.

label: paragraph_title
text: CANTON'S TREATMENT OF FOREIGNERS

label: text
text: NEED FOR TRENTINA.

label: text
text: What reads like a chapter from the early history of Canton in the days when foreign ships first appeared off the coast of the southern city and their crews went ashore to see the strange new land; is the news from Hongkong detailing the treatment of two British journalists who arrived at Canton on the British river steamer "Honum" on its first trip since the boycott was imposed. There on peaceful pursuits, the two men were quickly made the target of an ugly demonstration, surrounded by Whampoa endets with fixed bayonets, a heavy chain tightly clumped round their necks and were then imprisoned with fourteen Chinese strike-breakers. In the meanwhile crowds had gathered who clumored "Kill the foreigners," so incensed were they to find that two during Britons had entered the city. It was only with difficulty that the captors were persuaded to release the men and permit them to return to Shameen. The captives returned to safe territory to the accompaniment of profuse apologises on the part of the Chinese who excused themselves on the grounds that an ignorant, undisciplined mob was responsible.

label: text
text: This incident is but one of many proving conclusively (says the Shanghai Times") that Canton hasn't changed much in sentiment towards foreigners during the past hundred years or more. British pioneers in the latter part of the eighteenth century met with identical treatment as did the two British journalists, and the pages of history dealing with the early landing of foreigners in Canton are filled with the same type of incidents. It was this type of thing that made treaties with China absolutely necessary if China was to trade with other nations and if other nationals were to be guaranteed the slightest modicum of protection. At that time treaties guaranteeing such protection were necessary, and a necessary precaution which the years have in no way tended to destroy. Today they are as essential to the safe conduct of trade and legitimate business intercourse as they were in the eighteenth century. Those idealists who deny this do so simply because they are in complete ignorance of the facts, and are unable to appreciate the fact that Canton in 1925 is little removed from the Canton of Lord Macartney's day. What is true of Canton is true in somewhat lesser extent of other sections of China where anti-foreignism has been permitted to breed. A careful reading of the so-called 'inequal' travel will reveal that they are founded upon a basis of just protection for foreigners.
